That brown fat needs to reduce it's thermogenic energy generation rate when you have more body fat was a foregone conclusion. Why? Thermodynamics! The surface area to volume ratio of the human body sets the rate at which you lose heat to the environment. Heat flows out of your body proportionaly to the surface area, and the "reserve" of heat energy is proportional to your total mass, i.e. volume. The lower your surface area/volume ratio, the more slowly you lose heat to the environment.

This matters because as you get fatter, your surface are to volume ratio decreases. Yes you get a bigger surface area, but not as quickly as you gain volume. Think of a sphere: Area ~ r^2 , Volume ~r^3 . Essentially, this means fatter people need less thermogenic energy to maintain their internal body temperature because they lose heat more slowly to the environment. If fatter people had the same thermogenic energy consumption rate (per unit volume) as thinner people, they would cook from the inside out because they could not get rid of the waste heat fast enough. So the body has a mechanism to regulate this (doy- we're all mamals). Again, the cool bit is that the scientists found the specific protein that did it, not that it happens at all.

So fun facts: The technique scientists use to search for brown fat deposits in mammals (non-invasively, e.g. the tests that we run on living humans) is to feed them food with specially treated (mildly radioactive tracers) fats. If the subject is rapidly metabolizing fat, the radioactive tracers will be concentrated in the tissue responsible and can be picked up with a scan.

Why didn't these studies find brown fat deposits in adult humans? The answer is that they did find brown fat in a small sub-population of adult humans, who where lean and athletic. That was a bit of a mystery for a bit, but this study is actually one of the keys that solves the puzzle.

Why is it hard to find brown fat in adults? Two factors combined, they used Americans in the studies and as we have just learned in this article: being fat turns the metabolism of brown fat off. The radioactive tracers used to search for brown fat will only be observable if the brown fat cells are active. American adults are a rather over weight sample population and now we know that their brown fat cells are mostly deactivated as a result of being fat.
